steps.label: Situation
steps.body: A physical therapist has two goals for patients: (1) get more enjoyment from the challenge of developing physical skills, and (2) spend more time practicing those skills.

steps.label: Analysis
steps.body:
Meeting the first goal will bring about the second. If patients enjoy the challenge more, they will practice more.

Goal 1 achieved → Goal 2 achieved

steps.label: Evaluate / Goal
steps.body:
The analysis is a causal claim about two goals held by the same party: get the first one, and the first one helps produce the second. So every answer gets the same test. Suppose this party fully meets its first goal. Does that plausibly push the second goal forward?

Notice how low the bar is. The stem asks whether the analysis "could be appropriate," so the link does not have to be guaranteed. Four answers will have a first goal that makes the second more likely.

The exception is the situation where meeting the first goal does nothing for the second, or even makes the second pointless. Look for two goals that pull in different directions.

notes.body: Understanding the principles is what makes applying them possible. A student who really grasps the ideas is more likely to use them outside class. Meeting the first goal helps bring about the second, so the analysis could fit here.

Customers who are more satisfied with the product are plausibly customers who find it easier to use, and those customers place fewer calls asking how to use it. The link is not certain, but the stem only asks whether the analysis could be appropriate. It could.

A borrowed book that is lost or stolen can never be returned on time. Cutting the number of lost and stolen books puts more books back on the shelf, which pushes the on-time number up. Success with the first goal helps the second, so the analysis fits.

Run the test. The company wants "to construct a new, larger warehouse," and it wants employees to plan how "the old warehouse will be expanded to meet any need for more space." Suppose the first goal succeeds and the new, larger warehouse goes up. That new space meets the need for more space, so it gives the company less reason to expand the old warehouse, not more. Success with the first goal does not bring about the second, so the analysis could not be appropriate here.

On an EXCEPT question built around a pattern like this, state the test once (does goal 1 help produce goal 2?), run it on every choice, and keep the one that fails.

A more varied repertoire gives people who skipped the old lineup a reason to come. Variety is a plausible route to attracting new patrons, so meeting the first goal could help bring about the second. The analysis fits.

why: Choice notes were in the PT157/158 register (an em dash, repeated pattern talk, E misnames "new patrons" as audience members) and the combined Evaluate / Goal step gave no usable test for an EXCEPT question.

steps.label: Wildlife Commission Conclusion
steps.body: Future wetland development in Figoria must be regulated and offset by replacement habitats so that there is no net reduction of wetlands and no threat to species.

steps.label: Wildlife Commission Evidence
steps.body: Wetland development in industrialized nations has endangered many species.

steps.label: Development Commission Conclusion
steps.body: Figoria should be allowed to develop its wetlands.

steps.label: Development Commission Evidence
steps.body: Figoria has already conserved (unlike other nations that flagrantly developed wetlands), the development might not affect wildlife, and it is necessary for growth. Figoria has the same right to govern its own resources as nations that already used theirs commercially.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with what the two commissions actually disagree about. The Wildlife Commission wants regulation now: wetland development elsewhere has endangered species, so Figoria should require replacement habitats before any harm shows up at home. The Development Commission wants to develop without that requirement, and its best factual point is that Figorian development "might not affect wildlife." Figoria has conserved, and nobody has shown that its development is hurting anything.

So the fight is over timing. Should Figoria regulate in advance, based on what happened in other nations, or wait until harm is shown in Figoria? A principle that says regulation has to wait for demonstrated harm would settle that fight in the Development Commission's favor.

Also watch the direction of the stem. We need a principle that helps the Development Commission against the Wildlife Commission. An answer that supports protecting wildlife, however reasonable it sounds, is on the wrong side.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Two shapes would work. The first targets the timing fight: regulation should come only after development has been shown to harm wildlife. The Development Commission's evidence (no harm shown, development "might not affect wildlife") would then block the regulation the Wildlife Commission wants.

The second targets the fairness point: a nation that has conserved its resources has the same right to develop them as nations that already used theirs commercially.

The correct answer does not have to use every premise. It just has to start from something the Development Commission has given us and lead to allowing development or to holding off on regulation.

notes.body: The Development Commission claims Figoria has "as much right to govern our own resources" as other countries. Handing regulation to an international agreement takes that right away, and the trigger, endangered wildlife, is the Wildlife Commission's whole case. A works against the side it is supposed to help.

The Development Commission's case rests partly on growth, which is an economic need. B says the right of future generations to preserved wildlife outranks "the economic needs of individual nations," so that appeal loses. This is a principle the Wildlife Commission would cite, not the Development Commission.

C says regulation should happen only when a reduction of endangered species by commercial development "has been found." Flip that around: if no such reduction has been found, no regulation yet. The Development Commission says Figoria has conserved and that its development "might not affect wildlife," so no harm has been found in Figoria. The Wildlife Commission wants regulation before any harm, based on damage in other nations. C rules that out.

That is the move when a principle question asks you to support one side against the other: find the exact point where the two sides split, then pick the principle whose condition the favored side's evidence satisfies.

This is the trap, picked by 12%. It talks about how different nations have harmed the environment to different degrees. That's the Development Commission's theme, so it feels like their answer. But read what it concludes: regulation cannot allow for those differences. The commission's whole complaint is that Figoria's record of conserving should count. D says it doesn't.

Developing wetlands depletes a natural resource. If further depletion is "imprudent," the development the commission is asking for is imprudent too. E gives the Wildlife Commission a reason to restrict development, which is the opposite of what we need.

why: Evaluate put an invented paraphrase in quotation marks and never named the point of disagreement, the Goal named only the task, and A, B and E were one-line verdicts.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Most taxpayers and their families have few opportunities to use public libraries because they are only open at times when most children are at school and most adults are at work.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body:
No new taxes supporting the library system should be approved unless the library hours are changed to better suit taxpayers and their families.

"Unless" introduces the requirement. Diagrammed:
approve new library taxes → hours changed to suit taxpayers
hours not changed → no new library taxes

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence is about access: most taxpayers have few chances to use the libraries. The conclusion is a rule about taxes. Nothing in the argument says that whether taxpayers can use a facility has anything to do with whether a tax to support it should be approved.

Ask how we could still argue for the tax. Maybe the libraries serve the public in other ways, through online services, archives or school programs, so the tax is worth approving even if few taxpayers can walk in during open hours. Unless something ties tax approval to taxpayers' opportunities to use the facility, the conclusion does not follow.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for a principle that puts taxpayers' opportunity to use the facility on the required side of tax approval:

approve a new tax for a facility → most taxpayers can actually use it

Our evidence says most taxpayers cannot use the libraries much under the current hours. Run that through the principle and new library taxes are blocked until something, like the hours, changes.

Watch for the reversal. An answer that says when taxes should be approved (more convenient → approve the tax) has the same pieces on the wrong sides.

notes.body: A says these facilities "should be made as convenient as possible" for taxpayers. That is a goal for the libraries, but our conclusion is a rule about when new taxes may be approved. Ask what A can prove: only that libraries should be convenient. It never mentions taxes, so it cannot produce "no new taxes."

B is the reversal, and the most tempting answer because it uses the same pieces. B says: made more convenient → new taxes should be approved. The politician needs: new taxes approved → hours changed to be more convenient. B would let us approve a tax after the hours change. It says nothing about refusing the tax while the hours stay the same, which is the politician's actual claim.

C says taxpayers with "plenty of opportunities" to use a facility should have to pay taxes for it. Our taxpayers have few opportunities, so C's condition is not met and C tells us nothing about them. Concluding that they therefore should not pay would be negating C's condition, which C does not allow.

D is a claim about method: changing the hours is "the best way to increase usage." Even if that is true, it gives no reason to tie a tax to the change. The conclusion is about when a tax may be approved, and D never mentions taxes.

E says a new tax for a public facility should be approved "only when most taxpayers have ample opportunities to use that facility." So: approve the tax → most taxpayers have ample opportunities. The evidence says most taxpayers have few opportunities because of the hours. Contrapositive: no ample opportunities → no new tax. Until the hours change, the tax is blocked, which is the politician's conclusion.

Notice why E works and B does not. "Only when" and the politician's "unless" both put opportunity on the required side. E talks about any "public facility," and that is fine: a general principle covers the library as one case of it.

why: Choice notes were in the PT157/158 register (em dashes, 85+ words of repetition) and missed the key teaching about which side of the conditional opportunity belongs on; the Conclusion step moved the "should" and the Evaluate did not name the real gap.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Something that one is committed to might be either good or bad. Commitment to a relationship that benefits none of the people involved deserves no praise. Often, commitment is nothing more than involvement that has outlasted its original justification.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: All commitments should be seen as morally neutral.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Look at how far the conclusion reaches. The essayist says all commitments should be seen as morally neutral. The evidence is that what one is committed to "might be either good or bad," that one kind of commitment (to a relationship that benefits nobody) "deserves no praise," and that commitment is "often" just involvement that has outlasted its original justification.

Every piece of evidence covers some commitments. The conclusion covers all of them, including a commitment to a relationship that benefits everyone involved. Why would one unpraiseworthy commitment make that one neutral? The argument never says. That is the gap: from some to all.

So a principle that only covers the commitments described in the evidence will fall short. It has to do the generalizing for us.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for a principle whose condition is met by the evidence and whose outcome says something about all commitments:

some commitments deserve no praise → all commitments are morally neutral

An answer that only makes one kind of commitment neutral proves the conclusion for a subset. Eliminate it.

notes.body: A runs backward. It says: morally neutral → outlasted its justification or deserves no praise. Our evidence gives us commitments that deserve no praise and wants to reach neutrality, but neutrality sits on A's left side, so A can never prove it.

B says commitment is virtuous "when, but only when, the relationship or career is good." So a commitment to a good relationship is virtuous. That is not morally neutral, so B actually contradicts the claim that all commitments are morally neutral. It weakens the argument.

C is the tempting one, because it gets the direction right: deserves no praise → morally neutral. Apply it. The evidence gives us one kind of commitment that deserves no praise, so C makes that kind neutral. Now test the conclusion with a commitment that benefits everyone and does deserve praise. C says nothing about it. We needed all commitments, and C only reaches the unpraiseworthy ones.

D fails twice. Commitment is only "often" involvement that has outlasted its justification, so D covers some commitments, not all. And "cannot be virtuous" is not "morally neutral"; a commitment that is not virtuous could still be bad.

E says: if any commitment is undeserving of praise → all commitments are morally neutral. The evidence supplies the condition: a commitment to a relationship that benefits none of the people involved "deserves no praise." So all commitments are morally neutral, which is the conclusion word for word.

E works because it does the jump from some to all that C and D could not. When a conclusion says "all" and the evidence covers only some, the correct principle has to make that jump itself.

why: No Goal step, Evaluate never named the some-to-all gap and had a typo, and the notes were in the PT157/158 register; B's note missed that B actually contradicts the conclusion.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The filmmaker's subjects remain unaware of the camera's location and therefore act naturally.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The filmmaker's documentaries are more worthwhile than other documentaries such as those where people speak directly to the camera.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body: The argument shifts from evidence about subjects acting naturally to a conclusion about how worthwhile a documentary is. But there could easily be other factors which influence how worthwhile a documentary is. Maybe the most worthwhile documentaries are about events that impact a large number of people. Maybe those are more worthwhile even if the people who appear in the documentary are speaking directly to the camera and not behaving in a way that's completely natural. We can strengthen this argument by stating that documentaries in which people act naturally are more worthwhile than other documentaries. (act naturally → more worthwhile)

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for a principle with natural behavior on the left and "more worthwhile" on the right. It may say "authentic" instead of "natural." A documentary whose subjects act naturally depicts them authentically, so that is the same idea in different words.

A principle can only prove what is on its right side. Any answer that never reaches "worthwhile" cannot prove this conclusion, however closely it talks about cameras.

notes.body: A's outcome is that such a documentary "can be legitimate." The conclusion is a ranking: the filmmaker's documentaries are "more worthwhile" than others. Saying a kind of documentary can be legitimate does not put it above anything. A also only covers documentaries with "no purpose other than" authentic depiction, and we do not know that describes these.

B is the trap, because it mentions subjects speaking directly to a camera. Look at what B can prove: it says what authenticity requires (authentic → no subjects speaking to the camera). That could support a claim about which documentaries are not authentic. It never mentions worthwhile, so even if we granted that the other documentaries are less authentic, we would still need authenticity → worthwhile. B leaves the real gap open.

C addresses whether filmmakers owe their subjects the location of the cameras. That is an ethics question nobody in the argument raised. Whether hidden cameras are permissible tells us nothing about whether the resulting documentaries are more worthwhile.

D says: the more authentically a documentary depicts its subjects, the more worthwhile it is. The filmmaker's subjects act naturally because they do not know where the camera is, so the documentary depicts them authentically. In documentaries where people speak directly to the camera, the subjects know they are being filmed, and the filmmaker says people behave differently when they are aware of it. More authentic depiction, so more worthwhile.

Notice that the principle is comparative (the more of one, the more of the other), which is exactly what a comparative conclusion ("more worthwhile than") needs.

E tells subjects what they should do about finding the cameras. The conclusion is about the worth of the films, and E says nothing about worth. Even if every subject followed E, we still would not know these documentaries are more worthwhile.

why: Choice notes were in the PT157/158 register (em dashes, 85+ words of repetition, B's note confused about what B requires) and there was no separate Goal step naming the answer.

steps.label: Principle
steps.body: If someone buys an item, gets all of the use from it they intended to get, and returns it, then they are acting in an unethical way: `buy, use fully, and return → unethical`

steps.label: Evidence in Application
steps.body: James bought a video camera and returned it to the store two weeks later.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The return was unethical.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion, "unethical," matches the principle's outcome. So the question is whether the principle's conditions are all met. The principle needs three things: the person bought the item, got all the use from it they ever intended to get, and then returned it.

The application gives us the first and the last. James bought the camera and returned it. The middle condition is missing. Two weeks of ownership tells us nothing about whether James was finished with the camera. Maybe it broke. Maybe it was the wrong model. Without the middle condition, the principle cannot fire.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer showing that James got all the use from the camera that James ever intended to get before returning it. The cleanest version tells us what the camera was bought for and that this purpose was finished before the return.

notes.body: A shows a lot of use: James used the camera "extensively." A lot of use is not all the intended use. James might have planned to film for years, and the family recordings could be a small part of that. The principle's middle condition is still unproven.

B gives us both halves of the missing condition. It tells us the camera's whole purpose (to avoid hiring a professional videographer for one party) and that James returned it "immediately after the party." The one use James intended was finished, and then the camera went back. Bought, fully used, returned: the principle fires and the return is unethical.

That is the move on these questions: list the principle's conditions, check which ones the application already gives you, and find the answer that supplies the missing one.

C says James used the camera "several times" and returned it after it was dropped and some features stopped working. That does not show James got all the intended use. If anything, the damage cut the use short. The principle's middle condition is not met, so the principle says nothing about this return.
D gives a price reason for the return. It does not tell us whether James used the camera at all, let alone got all the intended use from it. The principle's middle condition stays unproven.

E is the most tempting wrong answer. It says James used the camera for the kind of use it was bought for, but using an item the way you meant to is not the same as getting all the use you ever meant to get. Someone who buys a camera for a year of weekend filming is using it as intended after one weekend, but is far from done. And E says James thought "a different one might work better," which suggests James still wanted a camera for future filming. The intended use was not finished.

why: Steps and notes used gendered pronouns for James, the step label and Goal had typos, and the notes were in the PT157/158 register with em dashes; C's note claimed the principle treats damaged returns as legitimate, which it does not say.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Some of the rare pygmy bears should be moved from their native island to the neighboring island.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body: This move represents the only viable chance of saving these valuable animals.

steps.label: Evidence (since)
steps.body: The bears risk extinction from the loss of habitat on their native island. The neighboring island is the only place that has a similar habitat.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The facts get us a long way. The bears risk extinction, and moving them is the only viable chance of saving them. But the conclusion is a "should," and nothing in the argument says we should do whatever it takes to save a species.

How could we argue against the move even granting every premise? Maybe the bears would wipe out something on the neighboring island. Maybe the move costs more than it is worth. The argument has no answer to those objections, because it never gives a principle saying that preventing extinction is what we should do.

So we need a principle that turns the fact that this is the only way to save an endangered species into the claim that we should do it. Because the conclusion says "should," the principle's outcome has to say "should" too. A principle that says the move is allowed, or that one requirement is met, will not get there.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
The typical correct answer here has the form If evidence, then conclusion. Look for something like:

species faces extinction + this action is its best chance → the action should be taken

The correct answer may use broader words ("a species," "whatever is most likely to prevent the extinction"), but its condition must be met by our facts, and its outcome must be a "should."

notes.body: A ranks species against each other. The argument never compares pygmy bears with any other species. Even if some species deserve more protection, A does not tell us these bears are among them, or that any particular action should be taken for them.

B is the trap, because it uses the argument's word "similar." B says rare animals should not be moved "unless these habitats are similar." That is a requirement: moved → habitats similar. Our habitats are similar, so the requirement is met. But meeting a requirement does not mean the move should happen. B removes one objection to the move; it cannot produce "should be moved."

C says: species in danger of extinction → do whatever is most likely to prevent the extinction. The bears risk extinction, so the condition is met. The move is "the only viable chance of saving these valuable animals," so it is the option most likely to prevent the extinction. C's outcome says it "should be undertaken," which is the conclusion.

Check both sides when you test a principle: our facts trigger the left side, and the right side delivers the conclusion's "should."

D says rarer species deserve more protection. The bears are rare, so D says more should be done for them. But doing more for a species does not tell us which action to take. D never gets us to moving the bears to the neighboring island.

E's condition fits, since the bears' habitat is being lost, but its outcome is that trying to find a new habitat is "permissible." Permissible means allowed. The argument says the bears should be moved, and permission to do something cannot prove that we should do it.

why: The Conclusion step was damaged text, the Evaluate only listed premises without naming the gap, and the notes were in the PT157/158 register (em dashes, 100+ words of repetition).

steps.label: Evidence (since)
steps.body:
Global warming has caused permafrost to melt under several arctic villages, forcing all their inhabitants to relocate at great expense.
Pollution from automobiles is a major contributor to global warming.

steps.label: Conclusion (should)
steps.body: The automotive industry should be required to help pay for the villagers' relocation.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The argument gives us evidence about automobiles contributing to a problem, then jumps to a conclusion claiming that the automobile industry should be required to help pay for that problem. This is an incredibly common pattern in Principle Strengthen questions. Regardless of whether or not that recommendation sounds reasonable, logically there is an important missing link in the argument.
For the argument to be valid, we need a premise to actually state that, if pollution from automobiles is a major cause of the village inhabitants needing to relocate, then the automotive industry should be required to help pay for the relocation.
```
autos are a cause → auto industry should pay
```

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
We're looking for an answer that makes this missing connection. Since the correct answer only needs to justify the argument, it doesn't have to match our prediction word for word, but it often comes close, so this question type is good practice for sharpening your predictions.

Check two things on every answer. Is the left side something Mateo actually established (automobile use contributes to the damage)? Does the right side say the automotive industry should pay? Beware of answers that add a condition Mateo never established, put the duty on a different party, or reverse the logic. Eliminate any answer that puts the industry paying on the left side (the sufficient condition).

notes.body: A only covers damage the industry "should have known would result from its activities." Mateo never says the automotive industry should have known its pollution would melt permafrost under these villages. A's condition is not established, so A cannot fire.

B is about how goods should be produced: in a way that "minimizes harm." Mateo's conclusion is about paying for a relocation. A rule about how to manufacture cannot prove a duty to pay for damage already done.

C is about when governments should pay: government required to pay → manufacturers also required. Mateo never says any government is required to pay for the relocation, so C's condition is not met, and C never gets us to the automotive industry paying.

D says: an industry whose product's use contributes to costly damage for others → that industry is liable for the damage. Check the condition against Mateo's facts. Automobile use produces pollution, a major contributor to global warming, which melted the permafrost and forced a costly relocation. Condition met. Outcome: the industry is liable, which covers "help pay."

D's outcome is a little stronger than Mateo's conclusion (liable for the damage, not just help pay). That is fine on a justify question. A principle can prove more than the conclusion needs; it just cannot prove less.

E's "only if" makes the general obligation a requirement: required to pay for specific damage → general obligation to pay for all damage produced by global warming. Mateo never establishes that general obligation, and even if Mateo had, a requirement being met would not prove the industry should pay. E can only block the conclusion, never prove it.

why: Choice notes were 100 to 150 words in the PT157/158 register with em dashes, E's note misdescribed the choice ("all damage its products cause" instead of all damage produced by global warming), and the Goal had a typo.
